# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 15 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 15

---

**1** But you, our God, are gracious and true, patient, and ordering all things in mercy.

**2** For even if we sin, we are yours, knowing your power; but we will not sin, knowing that we are counted as yours.

**3** For to know you is complete righteousness, and to know your power is the root of immortality.

**4** For neither did the evil device of men lead us astray, nor the fruitless labor of painters — a form daubed with varied colors,

**5** the sight of which stirs fools to longing, and they yearn for the breathless form of a lifeless image.

**6** Lovers of wicked things and worthy of such hopes are those who make such things, who desire them, who worship them.

**7** For a potter, kneading soft earth, laboriously shapes each vessel for our service; and from the same clay he fashions both the vessels that serve clean purposes and those that serve the opposite — all alike; but which particular use each shall serve is determined by the potter himself.

**8** And with miserable toil he forms from the same clay a god of no worth — he who was made of earth a little while before, and will return to that same earth a little while hence, when the debt of his soul is called in.

**9** But his concern is not that he will wear himself out, nor that his life is brief; but he competes with the goldsmith and the silversmith, and imitates the caster of bronze, and counts it an honor to mold counterfeit things.

**10** His heart is ashes, and his hope more worthless than dirt, and his life more dishonorable than clay,

**11** because he failed to know his Maker, him who breathed into him an active soul and inspired the breath of life.

**12** But he has regarded our life as mere play, and our existence as a marketplace for gain; for he says one must make profit from every source, even from evil.

**13** For above all others who err, this man knows that he sins — he who from earthly matter fashions fragile vessels and carved images.

**14** But most foolish of all, and more wretched than the soul of an infant, are the enemies of your people who held them in bondage.

**15** For they counted all the idols of the nations as gods — things that have no use of eyes for seeing, nor nostrils for drawing breath, nor ears for hearing, nor fingers for grasping, and whose feet are incapable of walking.

**16** For a man made them, and one whose breath is borrowed fashioned them; for no human being is able to mold a god like himself.

**17** For being mortal, he makes a dead thing with lawless hands; for he himself is better than what he worships, since he at least has had life, but they have never had it.

**18** And furthermore, they worship the most loathsome of living creatures; compared in senselessness, these are worse than all others,

**19** nor are they beautiful enough that one might find them desirable — yet these creatures have been passed over by God's blessing and praise.

---

**Council Notes:**

The chapter shifts from critique of Egypt to an affirmation of Israel's relationship with God (vv. 1–3), then returns to the absurdity of idol-making, culminating in the potter passage (vv. 7–13) — the most rhetorically developed section.

V. 7: The potter passage deliberately echoes Genesis 2:7 (God forming the human from clay). The author applies the potter's logic to idol-making to expose its absurdity: the same clay makes pots for clean use and unclean use, and the potter decides — yet the idolater treats his clay product as god.

V. 8: "the debt of his soul is called in" — Greek ἀπαιτηθῇ τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς χρέος. The image of life as a loan to be repaid at death is Hellenistic. LOGOS's "called in" is precise and retained.

V. 11: "breathed into him an active soul" (EMET) vs. "breathed into him an active soul" (LOGOS) vs. "blew the breath of life through him" (PNEUMA). The Greek ἐμπνεύσαντα ψυχὴν ἐνεργοῦσαν echoes the Genesis creation account. "Active soul" is retained from EMET/LOGOS.

V. 16: "one whose breath is borrowed" — a striking phrase. PNEUMA retains the original vivid logic: the craftsman himself depends on borrowed life, and cannot give life to what he makes.

Vv. 18–19: The reference to animal worship points toward Egypt specifically, setting up the antithesis of chapter 16. The ending of v. 19 is textually uncertain; LOGOS's rendering of the animals being "excluded from God's blessing" is adopted in modified form: "passed over by God's blessing and praise."
